newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya reform group united, to continue mass action.
newsitem.headline: Kenya reform group united, to continue mass action.

text.p: An opposition-backed alliance pressing for constitutional changes in Kenya emerged united from a crucial meeting on Tuesday and said it would present a reform agenda to President Daniel arap Moi's office on Wednesday.

The meeting featured the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) and opposition members of parliament. It was called after sharp differences over how to respond to a package of minimum constitutional reforms from the ruling KANU party.

"The institutional framework that the pro-reform movement will use for dialogue with the government and the ruling party on the constitutional, legal and administrative reforms is the National Convention Assembly (NCA)," said Kivutha Kibwana.
"Dialogue will be undertaken through NCA's National Convention Executive Council and any of its appropriate committees," added Kibwana, a leading NCA/NCEC official.

"This meeting resolves that the NCA...documents on reforms be presented to the government and president through the president's office on 23 July by representatives of the NCA and leaders of political parties," Kibwana added.

The NCA/NCEC is a coalition of political parties, human rights bodies, civic groups and churches that had united Kenya's squabbling political parties in a rare show of unity in demanding reforms before presidential and parliamentary polls.
But that unity was sorely tested by Moi's agreeing to meet opposition parties this week and by the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party agreeing to some reforms last week.
No date has been set for this year's general election but some opposition parties fear Moi wants to call it shortly after bills are approved by parliament, where KANU has a majority.

The meeting was also attended by parliamentary opposition leader Michael Kijana Wamalwa, who met Moi on security and reforms last week, and who was due to hold further meetings with the president on the subject this week.
All key leaders of opposition political parties were among the 105 people, including 57 parliament members, who attended.

"It was the single most unifying meeting of the NCA," said the Reverend Timothy Njoya, a Presbyterian minister whose arm was broken by police when they moved to stop a pro-reform rally in Nairobi and Kenyan provinces on July 7.
At least nine people were killed across Kenya after police moved in to stop rallies called by the NCA to press for constitutional reforms. Many of the parliament members were severely beaten.
"The people here represent true governance, represent a democratic government," Njoya told a news conference.
Kibwana said the meeting had resolved to continue "mass action" until the government agreed to "bona fide dialogue".
That meant an inter-denominational prayer service and a rally in the coastal resort of Mombasa would go ahead at the weekend and further action would be announced later.
Mombasa, Kenya's second city, is the coast centre of its tourism industry, the country's main foreign exchange earner.
Following the worst political unrest in Kenya in seven years, KANU which is led by Moi, offered its package of reforms and a constitutional review, which would end after the polls.
Attorney-General Amos Wako said on Friday he had began work on draft legislation which would be ready in two weeks.
One bill would give the president powers to appoint a commission to review the entire constitution, he said.
The second would repeal or amend 11 laws the opposition says are oppressive. The bills would be presented to the cabinet for approval before being tabled in parliament, Wako said.

But Kibwana said on Tuesday: "Until bonafide dialogue is undertaken by government, it should stop unilateral steps like drafting bills on legal and administrative reforms since these can only be developed after dialogue is concluded."
